summary: Updates the Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME so the structure linking a certificate to a signature is not hardwired to SHA-1. It defines a new attribute allowing algorithm agility. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When an S/MIME message is signed, the signature also records which certificate was used, so that a recipient can tell the right certificate from another one with the same key. This RFC changes that record so it can use a stronger hash than SHA-1, and adds a new attribute for it while keeping the old one.

questions: why replace sha-1 in s/mime signatures
subtitle: Letting an S/MIME signature name the hash that identifies the signing certificate.

tldr.problem: The Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME tie a signed message to its signing certificate with a hash, and that structure is fixed to SHA-1, whose collision attacks are now practical.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a second certificate identifier, ESSCertIDv2, which carries the name of the hash algorithm next to the hash, and a new signed attribute, SigningCertificateV2, that uses it.
tldr.outcome: A signer can identify its certificate with SHA-256 or a stronger hash, and the old SigningCertificate attribute stays in place so that software that only knows SHA-1 still works.

today: RFC 5035 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 2634 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated, so the version 2 attribute and the version 1 attribute are both still defined as they are here.

sections.title: Why the Change Was Needed
sections.content:
In the original Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME, RFC 2634, a structure was defined for cryptographically linking a certificate to the signature that was used in validation. That structure is called ESSCertID, and it identifies a certificate by its hash. The structure is hardwired to use a SHA-1 hash value. The recent attacks on SHA-1 mean that a new attribute is needed, one that allows other algorithms to be used.

This document defines the structure ESSCertIDv2 along with a new attribute, SigningCertificateV2, which uses the updated structure. Because the structure carries an algorithm identifier, the hash algorithm can be chosen at the time of signing. The document also specifies the continued use of ESSCertID, so that compatibility is kept when SHA-1 is used to tell certificates apart.

The document is written as a set of edits to RFC 2634. It replaces Section 5.4 of that RFC with a new structure in which the signing certificate attribute is defined in two versions, and the ASN.1 module in the appendix of RFC 2634 is replaced with the one given here.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed message carries a note saying which certificate signed it. That note was a SHA-1 hash, and SHA-1 hashes can now be made to collide on purpose. This RFC lets the note name the hash it used, so a stronger hash can be used instead, and it keeps the old form working.

sections.title: Two Attributes, and the Cases to Handle
sections.content:
The signing certificate attribute exists to prevent simple substitution and re-issue attacks and to allow a restricted set of certificates to be used when verifying a signature. Two attributes exist for this, because of a flaw in the original design. The only substantial difference between them is that SigningCertificateV2 allows the hash algorithm to be chosen, while SigningCertificate forces the SHA-1 hash algorithm. With the advances in the ability to create hash collisions for SHA-1, the document says it is wise to move forward sooner rather than later.

The rules for choosing between them are clear. When SHA-1 is used, SigningCertificate must be used. If any algorithm other than SHA-1 is used, SigningCertificateV2 must be used, and it should not be used for SHA-1. Applications should recognise both attributes for as long as they consider SHA-1 able to distinguish between two different certificates, that is, for as long as the possibility of a collision is sufficiently low. If both attributes appear in one message, they are evaluated independently.

The document sets out four cases to take into account when processing the attribute.

  • The signature validates and the hashes match. This is the success case.
  • The signature validates and the hashes do not match. The certificate holds the correct public key, but it is not the certificate the signer intended to be used. The application should look for a different certificate with the same public key whose hash does match, and if there is none, this is a failure.
  • The signature fails validation and the hashes match. The signature has been modified in some way, and this is a failure.
  • The signature fails validation and the hashes do not match. Either the signature has been modified or the wrong certificate was used. The application should look for a different certificate that matches the hash value in the attribute and use it to retry the signature validation.

In other words, the hash in the attribute and the certificate that verified the signature have to agree, and when they do not the verifier has to work out whether it is looking at the wrong certificate or at a modified signature.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two attributes now. The old one only works with SHA-1 and is still required for SHA-1. The new one takes any hash algorithm and is required for anything else. Checking a signature gives two answers: whether the signature itself is good, and whether the certificate matches the hash in the attribute.

sections.title: The SigningCertificateV2 Attribute
sections.content:
SigningCertificateV2 is identified by the object identifier {1 2 840 113549 1 9 16 2 47}, and its ASN.1 definition holds a sequence of certificate identifiers and, optionally, a sequence of policy information.

The certs field contains the list of certificates that are to be used in validating the message. The first certificate identified in the sequence must be the certificate used to verify the signature, and its encoding should include the issuerSerial field. That field may be omitted if other constraints ensure that issuerAndSerialNumber is present in the SignerInfo. If the hash of the certificate does not match the certificate used to verify the signature, the signature must be considered invalid.

If more than one certificate is present, the later ones limit the set of certificates that may be used during validation. They can be attribute certificates, which limit the authorizations that are honoured, or public key certificates, which limit path validation. The issuerSerial field should be present for these certificates unless the client validating the signature is expected to have easy access to all the certificates needed for validation. If only the signing certificate is present, there are no restrictions on the set of certificates used to validate the signature.

The policies field holds a sequence of policy information terms that identify the certificate policies the signer asserts apply to the certificate and under which the certificate should be relied upon. The value suggests a policy value to be used in the relying party's certification path validation, and the definition of PolicyInformation comes from RFC 3280.

If present, the attribute must be a signed attribute and must not be an unsigned attribute. A SignerInfo must not include multiple instances of the attribute, and the attribute must include only a single instance of AttributeValue: there must not be zero or several.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attribute lists the certificates that may be used to check the message. The first one has to be the certificate that actually made the signature, and if its hash does not match that certificate the signature is invalid. Any further certificates narrow what the verifier will accept. The attribute also lets the signer say which certificate policies apply.

sections.title: The ESSCertIDv2 Structure
sections.content:
How a certificate is identified is an often-discussed issue, and ESSCertIDv2 supplies two fields for it. The structure is a sequence of an algorithm identifier, a hash, and an optional issuer and serial number.

The hashAlgorithm field holds the identifier of the algorithm used to compute the hash. It defaults to SHA-256. The certHash field is computed over the entire DER-encoded certificate, including the signature. The hash is needed because the detection of a substituted certificate rests on the fact that a substituted certificate maps to a different hash value. Hashes are convenient because certificate stores often use them as a method of indexing and retrieving certificates.

The issuerSerial field holds the identification of the certificate by issuer and serial number, the method used in RFC 3280, where the issuer distinguished name must be present. That pair would normally be enough to identify the correct signing certificate, assuming the same issuer name is not reused across the set of trust anchors. The pair can also be stored in the sid field of the SignerInfo object, but the sid field is not covered by the signature, so where the pair is not used in the sid, or where it needs to be signed, it should be placed in the issuerSerial field of ESSCertIDv2.

Attribute certificates and additional public key certificates that carry information have no issuer and serial number pair represented anywhere in a SignerInfo object. When such a certificate is not included in the SignedData object, it becomes much harder to find the correct set of certificates from a hash alone, so those certificates should be identified by the IssuerSerial object. Within it, the issuer field holds the issuer name of the certificate: for a non-attribute certificate it must contain only the issuer name from the certificate, encoded in the directoryName choice of GeneralNames, and for an attribute certificate it must contain the issuer name field from the attribute certificate. The serialNumber field holds the serial number that uniquely identifies the certificate for that issuer.
sections.plainLanguage: The new identifier has three parts: which hash algorithm was used, the hash of the whole certificate including its signature, and, when it is needed, the name of the issuer and the serial number. The hash is what proves the certificate is the one the signer used; the issuer and serial number are the fallback for certificates that have no other way to be named.

sections.title: Keeping the Old Attribute Working
sections.content:
The document also inserts the original text of RFC 2634 as two new sections, with minor changes, so that the older form keeps working. The version 1 attribute, SigningCertificate, is identified by the object identifier {1 2 840 113549 1 9 16 2 12} and holds a sequence of ESSCertID structures together with an optional sequence of policy information. Its rules are the ones the version 1 section already described: the first certificate in the sequence must be the one used to verify the signature, its encoding should include the issuerSerial field, and if the hash does not match the certificate used to verify the signature, the signature must be considered invalid.

The version 1 certificate identifier, ESSCertID, is a sequence of a hash and an optional issuer and serial number. The hash is computed over the entire DER-encoded certificate, including the signature.

The ASN.1 module in the appendix of RFC 2634 is replaced by the one in this document, which is named ExtendedSecurityServices-2006 and carries the object identifier {1 2 840 113549 1 9 16 0 30}. It keeps the rest of the ESS definitions, such as the receipt request and the content hints, and adds the new structures.
sections.plainLanguage: The old attribute and the old certificate identifier stay in the document unchanged apart from small edits, and the ASN.1 module at the back of RFC 2634 is replaced by a new one that includes both the old and the new structures.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document exists to address the security problem of a substituted certificate being used by the validator. If a different certificate is used by the validator than the one the signer used, the validator may not get the right answer. The example given is a certificate that was revoked and replaced by a new certificate with the same public key issued to a different individual: because the issuer and serial number field is not protected, an attacker could replace it and point to the new certificate, and the validation would succeed.

The attributes defined in this document are to be placed in locations that are protected by the signature. The attribute gives no additional security if it is placed in an unsigned or unauthenticated location.

The attributes let a signer choose a hash algorithm to identify a certificate, and a poorly chosen one may give inadequate protection against certificate substitution or cause a denial of service for that protection. Using the same hash algorithm as the one used to sign the message lets the sender ensure that the attributes give security of a comparable strength. Since recipients must support the hash algorithm in order to verify the signature, choosing the same one also makes it more likely to be supported in the context of certificate identification. An unsupported hash algorithm does not stop the message being validated, but it does deny the recipient protection against certificate substitution.

Clients are permitted to include both ESSCertID and ESSCertIDv2 in the same message, so that legacy implementations still get protection against certificate substitution. Because the two attributes are generated and evaluated independently, their contents could conflict: where a signer has several certificates with the same public key, the two attributes could name different signing certificates, and the result of signature processing may then depend on which certificate is used. Recipients that evaluate both attributes may choose to reject such a message.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the attribute is to catch a validator being given a different certificate from the one the signer used, for example a renewed certificate that was issued to someone else. It only works if the attribute is inside the signed part of the message, and it works best when it uses the same hash algorithm that signed the message. Sending both the old and new attributes is allowed, but if they disagree a recipient may refuse the message.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CASES WHEN CHECKING A SIGNATURE

cells: The certificate is the one the signer used
The right public key, a different certificate
Look for another certificate with the same public key
The signature was modified or the wrong certificate was used
Look for a certificate matching the hash and retry
